title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**I.maṅgala**
Homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. A Concise Explanation of the padārtha (category, topic)s falling within the Ornament of Clear Realisation (abhisamaya (clear realisation)). The eight categories beginning with sarvākārajñatā (knowledge of all aspects, full omniscience of a buddha), and the seventy categories beginning with cittotpāda (arising of bodhicitta), are the subject-matter of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Here their nature is set forth saṃkṣepataḥ (in brief, concisely).
**I.intro**
The eight categories. They are: knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), mārgajñatā (knowledge of the paths of the three vehicles), sarvajñatā / vastujñatā (knowledge of the bases, the śrāvaka-level all-knowledge) (= knowledge of the bases), ākāra (aspect, mode)-full realisation (sarvākārābhisambodha), mūrdhābhisamaya (culminating, summit realisation), ānupūrvikābhisamaya (serial, gradual realisation), ekakṣaṇābhisambodha (realisation in a single instant), and the dharmakāya (Dharma-body of a buddha, with its four kāyas) — these eight categories are set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. As [it says]: // The Perfection of Wisdom is fully proclaimed by eight categories: knowledge of all aspects, knowledge of the paths, and then knowledge of [all] bases; // full realisation of all aspects, [the realisation] that has reached the summit, the serial [realisation], the realisation in a single instant, and the Dharma-body — these are the eight. //
**I.1**
1. Knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). Definition (lakṣaṇa (defining mark, definition)): the culminating knowledge that, in a single moment, directly and accurately realises the aspects of objects to their full extent — that is the definition of the knowledge of all aspects. Divisions (bheda (division, sub-type)): it has two — the knowledge [reaching] as far [as all aspects] (yāvaj-jñāna) and the knowledge [of things] as they are (yathāvaj-jñāna). The wisdom that knows all aspects without remainder is the yāvaj-jñāna; the wisdom that knows objects just as they are in their own nature is the yathāvaj-jñāna. Alternatively: the knowledge directly realising, without remainder, the aspects of the causes (beginning with the arising of bodhicitta) and of the uncontaminated fruits is one division; the twenty-two uncontaminated knowledges arising on the buddha-ground are the second division. Scope (avadhi (limit, scope (the stages over which a topic operates))): the knowledge of all aspects occurs solely on the buddha-ground.
**I.2**
2. Knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā). Definition: being a noble Mahāyāna realisation that is taken up by the wisdom directly realising the essencelessness of the three paths — that is the definition of the knowledge of the paths. Divisions: it has four — knowledge of the path of the śrāvakas, knowledge of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, knowledge of the Mahāyāna path, and the knowledge of all wisdom-and-means present in the continuum of a noble Mahāyāna practitioner. Scope: the range of the knowledge of the paths extends from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha-ground.
**I.3**
3. Knowledge of [all] bases (sarvajñatā), [glossed as] knowledge of the bases (vastujñatā). Definition: the knowledge present in a noble being's continuum, of the nature of a hīnayāna-type realisation, taken up by the wisdom that directly realises the selflessness of persons present in all dharmas — that is its definition. The knowledge present in a hīnayāna noble being's continuum directly realises emptiness, which is a synonym for the selflessness of persons; because it is taken up by that, the qualifier 'of hīnayāna type' is placed in the definition of the knowledge of bases. Divisions: it has two — being far from, and being near to, the resultant Mother of the Conquerors (jina-jananī, the Perfection of Wisdom). Scope: the range of the knowledge of bases extends from the śrāvaka path of seeing up to the buddha-ground.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**I.4**
4. Full realisation of all aspects (sarvākārābhisambodha). Definition: the yoga of [a heroic] being, taken up by the wisdom consisting of meditative cultivation, [directed at] the aspects of the trisarvajñatā (three [kinds of] omniscience, the three knowledges together) — that is its definition. Divisions: by its own nature, twenty prayoga (application, practice (esp. the four central abhisamayas))s; by aspect, the yogas that accomplish the 173 aspects connected with the three knowledges are the 173 divisions of this full realisation of all aspects. 'The yoga of a being,' 'the perfection that is the path,' 'the bodhisattva path,' 'the Mahāyāna practice,' 'the armour-practice' — these are synonyms. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**I.5**
5. Culminating realisation (mūrdhābhisamaya). Definition: the yoga of a being which is the highest peak in the cultivation of the aspects of the three knowledges — aspects taken up by the wisdom consisting of meditative cultivation with emptiness as its object, and established by the view of that [emptiness] — this culminating application (mūrdha-prayoga) is its definition. Because the applications taken up by the bodhisattva's wisdom consisting of hearing are also included right here, the definition adds the qualifier 'established by the view of that.' Divisions: in brief, four — the culminating application of the path of preparation, of the path of seeing, of the path of cultivation, and the uninterrupted culminating application. Or else: the four [stages] of the path of preparation called heat, summit, forbearance, and supreme dharma; plus three [more], namely [the culminating applications] of the paths of seeing and cultivation and the uninterrupted culminating application — making seven culminating applications. But in detail it should be understood that there are 173 culminating applications. Scope: its range extends from the heat-application of the Mahāyāna path of preparation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**I.6**
6. Serial realisation (ānupūrvikābhisamaya). Definition: the yoga of a being, established through repeated cultivation in order to make firm the aspects of the three knowledges — that serial application is its definition. Divisions: this serial realisation has thirteen. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the stage just prior to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**I.7**
7. Realisation in a single instant (ekakṣaṇābhisambodha). Definition: the final yoga of a being, arisen through serial cultivation in order to perfectly master the aspects of the three knowledges — that is its definition. Divisions: by way of differentiation it has four. Scope: this application occurs only at the stage of the bodhisattva in his last existence.
**I.8**
8. The Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Definition: the fruit arisen by the power of the highest cultivation of the aspects of the three knowledges — that is, the ultimate uncontaminated qualities — is the Dharma-body; this is its definition. Divisions: it has four — the essence-body (svabhāva-kāya), the wisdom Dharma-body (jñāna-dharmakāya), the enjoyment body (sāmbhogika-kāya), and the emanation body (nairmāṇika-kāya). Scope: this Dharma-body occurs solely on the buddha-ground.
**II.intro**
The seventy categories. Divided into three [groups], the seventy categories are expounded separately: the thirty dharmas that characterize the three knowledges, the thirty-six dharmas that characterize the four applications, and the four that characterize the Dharma-body — making seventy.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.intro**
1. The thirty dharmas characterizing the three knowledges. Among them: ten teach the knowledge of all aspects, eleven teach the knowledge of the paths, nine teach the knowledge of bases — making thirty. (a) The ten dharmas characterizing the knowledge of all aspects. They are: 1. the Mahāyāna arising of bodhicitta, 2. instruction (avavāda), 3. the limbs of penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya ([roots of good] conducive to penetration — heat, summit, forbearance, supreme dharma)), 4. the support of [Mahāyāna] practice, 5. the object of practice, 6. the aim of practice, 7. the armour-practice (sannāha-pratipatti (practice, undertaking)), 8. the engagement-practice, 9. the equipment-practice, 10. the issuing-forth practice — these ten dharmas characterize the knowledge of all aspects, as set forth in two verses of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Thus: // The arising of [bodhi]citta, instruction, and the fourfold limb of penetration; the support of practice, whose nature is the dharmadhātu; // the object, the aim, the armour and the engagement deeds, the equipments together with the issuing-forth — [these are] the Sage's knowledge of all aspects. //
**II.A.i.1**
1. The arising of bodhicitta (cittotpāda). Four things are to be known: its definition, divisions, object, and scope. All is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // The arising of bodhicitta is the longing for perfect awakening for the sake of others. It is stated both in brief and at length, and in accordance with the sūtra. // It is twenty-twofold: [likened] to earth, gold, the moon, fire, a treasure, a jewel-mine, the ocean, a diamond, a mountain, medicine, a [spiritual] friend, a wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, sweet song, a king, a treasury, a great highway, a vehicle, a fountain-spring of water, joyful proclamation, a river, and a cloud. // Definition: the special Mahāyāna mental consciousness, marshalled by an aspiration arising from its own cause, conjoined with the longing for awakening, for the sake of others — that is the definition of the arising of bodhicitta. Object: the arising of bodhicitta operates by taking as its object awakening for one's own sake and nirvāṇa present in others' continuums for the sake of others. Divisions: by nature it has two — the arising of bodhicitta that is by nature an aspiration to awakening (praṇidhi-citta), and that which is by nature engagement in awakening (prasthāna-citta). From the standpoint of the associated mental factors, it has twenty-two sub-types, namely [it is] like: 1. earth, 2. gold, 3. the moon, 4. fire, 5. a great treasure, 6. a jewel-mine, 7. the great ocean, 8. a diamond, 9. a mountain, 10. medicine, 11. a spiritual friend, 12. a wish-fulfilling gem, 13. the sun, 14. sweet song, 15. a king, 16. a granary, 17. a great highway, 18. a vehicle, 19. fountain-water, 20. joyful proclamation, 21. a river, and 22. a cloud. Scope: the arising of bodhicitta in bodhisattvas is fourfold: that grounded in resolute faith, on the ground of conduct through resolution; that with pure superior intention, on the seven [pure] grounds; that of [karmic] maturation, on the eighth and following [grounds]; and that free of obscuration, on the buddha-ground. As stated in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra: // That arising of bodhicitta [first] is by resolute faith; the next is with pure superior intention; on the [eighth and higher] grounds it is held to be of maturation; and likewise [the last is] free of obscuration. //
**II.A.i.2**
2. Instruction (avavāda). Its whole domain — definition, divisions, scope, and the rule for [who may] hear it — is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // [Instruction] is to be known in regard to practice, the [four] truths, the Three Jewels beginning with the Buddha, [the practice of] non-attachment, untiring [effort], full embrace of the path, // the five eyes, the six supernormal cognitions and their qualities, the path of seeing, and that called the path of cultivation — so instruction is tenfold. // Definition: the unerring teaching of the path of liberation is the definition of instruction. Or else: the unerring, pure teaching which is the means of attaining the goal sought, by way of the Mahāyāna arising of bodhicitta, is the definition of Mahāyāna instruction. Divisions: first, taking up non-decline so as to ripen qualities already attained, there is the instruction of training; thereafter, taking up the attainment of qualities not yet attained, there is the instruction of admonition — these are the two divisions. Again, by difference of object, instruction is to be known as tenfold. Thus: (1) instruction concerning practice (governed by [the two truths]); (2) instruction concerning the truths (the four noble truths, the object of practice); (3) instruction concerning the Three Jewels (the three refuges, the basis); (4) the teaching-instruction concerning non-attachment (the cause of progress to the distinguished [goal]); (5) the teaching-instruction concerning untiring effort (the cause of non-regressing progress); (6) instruction concerning full embrace of the path (the cause of progress on no other vehicle); (7) the instruction on the five eyes (the cause of not depending on another's conditions); (8) the instruction on the [six] supernormal cognitions (the cause of fulfilling the knowledge of all aspects); (9) the instruction concerning the path of seeing, which is the total uprooting, together with their seeds, of the imputed afflictions to be abandoned by seeing; (10) the instruction concerning the path of cultivation, which is the total uprooting, together with their seeds, of the innate obscurations to be abandoned by cultivation. Scope: its range extends from before entering the path up to the buddha-ground. Rule for hearing: even a person who has not entered the path, if he has pure superior intention and pure karma, is a fit vessel to hear Mahāyāna instruction; and the bodhisattva who has entered the path hears instruction, over many aeons, from buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.i.3**
3. The limb of penetration (nirvedhāṅga). The definition, divisions, scope, object, aspects, and so forth of the fourfold roots conducive to penetration — heat and the rest — are set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // By object, by aspect, by being a cause, and by full embrace, [these roots] have the conjunction of the four conceptions, each in its own way, for the holy ones who possess them. // The [roots] of heat and the rest, in their weak, middling, and strong [degrees], of the protecting bodhisattva are superior to those of the śrāvakas together with the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas]. // Definition: the realisation arising immediately after its own cause, the [roots] conducive to liberation, is the path of preparation — that is its definition. 'Path of preparation,' 'realisation of the meaning,' and 'limb of penetration' are synonyms. Divisions: there are three paths of preparation, for the three vehicles beginning with the śrāvaka. Within each of the three paths of preparation there are four divisions called heat, summit, forbearance, and supreme dharma. Thus the divisions of the path of preparation number twelve. As for the Mahāyāna path of preparation: its four roots conducive to penetration — heat, summit, forbearance, supreme dharma — are superior to the śrāvaka roots conducive to penetration by five distinctions. Each of these roots, in turn, is threefold by weak, middling, and strong; thus twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna path of preparation arise. Scope: the pervasion of the path of preparation extends from the attainment of insight-meditation, operating by taking as its object some one of the three [kinds of] selflessness, up to the attainment of [the first] ground. Object, aspects, etc.: the Mahāyāna path of preparation is superior to the hīnayāna path of preparation by six distinctions, namely: by distinction of object, of aspect, of being a cause, of full embrace, of conjunction with the conceptions to be abandoned, and of the division into weak, middling, and strong. And this superiority is lucidly explained in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in nine verses, beginning 'the object [is impermanence and so forth]' and ending 'the full embrace in every way.'
**II.A.i.4**
4. The support of practice (pratipatter ādhāra). The support of Mahāyāna practice is the natural lineage (gotra (spiritual lineage, disposition (the basis of practice))). Its definition and so forth is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // The basis of the sixfold realised dharma, of the antidote and the abandoning, of the application of the two, of wisdom together with compassion, // of being uncommon with the disciples, of [acting for] the welfare of others in sequence, and of effortlessly functioning knowledge — that basis is called the lineage. // Definition: in general, that dharmadhātu which, once purified, ripens into awakening is the lineage; this is its definition. In particular, that dharmadhātu which, once purified, ripens into unsurpassed perfect awakening, and which is the support of Mahāyāna practice — that is the natural lineage. Divisions: by way of designation there are two — the natural lineage and the developed lineage. The naturally abiding lineage which is the basis of Mahāyāna practice is thirteenfold from the standpoint of the dharmas based upon it. This very natural lineage is also the support of the Mahāyāna path of accumulation. [The thirteen:] the four supports of the four worldly roots conducive to penetration — heat, summit, forbearance, supreme dharma; one support [each] for the supramundane path of seeing and the supramundane path of cultivation — making six natural lineages. Then: the support of the practice of the antidote; the support of the practice of abandoning; the support of the path of release (which, through the non-apprehension of what is to be abandoned by the antidote, is free of the conceptions bound up with the arising and ceasing of that); the support of wisdom and compassion; the support of the dharma uncommon with śrāvakas and the rest; the support of [acting for] the welfare of others in sequence; and the support of effortlessly functioning knowledge — these are the thirteen divisions of the naturally abiding lineage. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment. In particular it should be understood that its pervasion extends from the heat-stage of the path of preparation explicitly indicated above, up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.i.5**
5. The object of practice (pratipatter ālambana). Three things are set forth here: the definition, divisions, and scope of the objects of practice. The nature of the object is shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // The object is all dharmas: namely the wholesome and the rest, those called worldly attainments and those held to be supramundane, the contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas, the conditioned and unconditioned, the dharmas common with the disciples, and those uncommon, [proper] to the Sage. // Definition: the very fact of being an object of knowledge for practice is its being an object — that is the definition. Divisions: the object is elevenfold. Thus: (1) the three — bodily action and the rest — that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; (2) the five aggregates connected with the immature ordinary person; (3) the four uncontaminated meditative absorptions included among all noble persons; (4) the five appropriating aggregates, as that which is not the antidote to the view of self; (5) the four uncontaminated applications of mindfulness, as the antidote to the view of self; (6) the conditioned [dharmas] beginning with the limbs of awakening, included in the desire-realm and the other realms dependent on causes and conditions (= the truth of the path); (7) the unconditioned [dharmas] beginning with suchness, which is independent of causes and not contained in the three realms (= the truth of cessation); (8–10) the qualities beginning with the four meditative absorptions that arise in the continuum of all noble persons; (11) the uncommon [dharmas] beginning with the ten powers, the properties arising in the continuum of a Perfectly Awakened One — so the object is elevenfold. Scope: by the sequence of realisation all dharmas are taken as objects accurately; hence it should be understood that there is no ground-limit to the objects.
**II.A.i.6**
6. The aim of practice (pratipatti-samuddeśa). Three things are to be known: its definition, divisions, and scope; they are indicated in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in this single verse. Thus: // By three greatnesses — in the triad of [the great] mind [intent on] the supremacy of all beings, of abandoning, and of realisation — the aim of the noble self-arisen ones is to be understood. // Definition: the very goal of the bodhisattva established in practice is the aim of practice — that is the definition. Divisions: it has three — the greatness of the mind [intent on] the supremacy of all beings, the greatness of abandoning, and the greatness of realisation. Scope: this aim is fully accomplished solely on the buddha-ground.
**II.A.i.7**
7. The armour-practice (sannāha-pratipatti). Its definition and so forth is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse, thus: // The armour-practice is that which, by way of comprising each of the six [perfections] within the sixfold [set of] giving and the rest — these are taught as six sets of six. // [Definition of Mahāyāna practice:] relying on the Mahāyāna arising of bodhicitta, for the accomplishment of unsurpassed perfect awakening, that activity which, in regard to the three knowledges in general, is grounded in the bright dharmas, and which, in each of the four realisations beginning with the full realisation of all aspects, is grounded in the six perfections — that is the definition of Mahāyāna practice. [Divisions of practice:] this Mahāyāna practice is fourfold, namely: the armour-practice, the engagement-practice, the equipment-practice, and the issuing-forth practice. Definition of the armour-practice: the yoga of a being, taken up by the wisdom that comprises [all] six perfections within each perfection, is the definition of the armour-practice. 'Armour-practice' and 'the bodhisattva path' are synonyms. Divisions: from the armour-practice of the perfection of giving up to the armour-practice of the perfection of wisdom, there are six divisions. Within giving too there are the six perfections — giving, morality, and so forth; so, since there are six sixes within the six perfections, in detail there are thirty-six divisions. Scope: its range extends from the bodhisattva on the path of accumulation up to the bodhisattva at the final moment.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.i.8**
8. The engagement-practice (prasthāna-pratipatti). Its nature is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // In the [four] meditative absorptions and formless [attainments], in giving and the rest, in the path, in loving-kindness and the rest, in the union of having-gone-beyond apprehension, in the threefold purity [of the three spheres], // in the aim, in the six supernormal cognitions, and in the way of the knowledge of all aspects — the engagement-practice, mounting up to the Mahāyāna, is to be known. // Definition: through practice in which cultivation predominates, the act of engaging in a Mahāyāna dharma — whether of the nature of cause or of fruit — is the definition of the engagement-practice. Divisions: this engagement-practice is to be known as ninefold, namely: engagement in the meditative-absorption and formless attainments; in the six perfections beginning with giving; in the noble paths; in the four immeasurables; in the union of non-apprehension; in the threefold purity [of agent, object, act]; in the threefold aim beginning with [the mind intent on] the supremacy of all beings; in the six supernormal cognitions; and in the knowledge of all aspects. Scope: its range extends from the heat-stage of the path of preparation on the ground of conduct through resolution, up to the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**II.A.i.9**
9. The equipment-practice (sambhāra-pratipatti). The whole of its definition and so forth is well set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // Compassion, the sixfold set beginning with giving, calm-abiding together with insight, the path that is the union [of the two], and the skill that is in means; // knowledge, merit, the path, retention-formulae, the ten grounds, and the antidote — such is the sequence of the equipment-practice, to be understood. // Definition: that activity which directly bestows the great awakening that is one's own fruit — such activity is the definition of the equipment-practice. Divisions: this equipment-practice has seventeen divisions, namely: the equipment of great compassion, of giving, of morality, of forbearance, of effort, of meditative absorption, of wisdom, of calm-abiding, of insight, of the union [of the two], of skill in means, of knowledge, of merit, of the path, of retention-formulae, of the [ten] grounds, and of the antidote. Scope: mere equipment occurs even on the ground of the beginner; but those equipments explicitly indicated as the means of attaining the great awakening occur from the supreme-dharma stage of the path of preparation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment. The first fifteen equipment-practices occur up to the supreme-dharma stage of the path of preparation; the sixteenth, the equipment of the [ten] grounds, and the seventeenth, the equipment of the antidote, occur on the ten grounds.
**II.A.i.10**
10. The issuing-forth practice (niryāṇa-pratipatti). Its nature is well shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // The issuing-forth in the aim, in sameness, in the welfare of beings, and in effortlessness; the issuing-forth toward the ultimate; the issuing-forth marked by attainment; // and the issuing-forth in the knowledge of all aspects, whose range is the path — the issuing-forth practice is to be known as eightfold. // Definition: the yoga of a being, belonging to the pure grounds, which definitively issues forth into omniscience, is the definition of the issuing-forth practice. Divisions: this issuing-forth practice is eightfold, namely: issuing-forth in the threefold aim, in sameness, in the welfare of beings, the effortless issuing-forth, the issuing-forth toward the ultimate, the issuing-forth of attainment, the issuing-forth in the knowledge of all aspects, and the issuing-forth in the path. Scope: its pervasion occurs only on the three pure grounds. // Thus the ten dharmas characterizing the knowledge of all aspects. //

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.ii.intro**
(ā) The eleven dharmas characterizing the knowledge of the paths. They are: 1. the limbs of the knowledge of the paths, beginning with the dimming [of the gods]; 2. the path of the śrāvakas; 3. the path of the pratyekabuddhas; 4. the bodhisattva path; 5. the function of the path of cultivation; 6. the resolute faith of the path of cultivation; 7. the praise, eulogy, and laudation of one with resolute faith on the path of cultivation; 8. dedication (pariṇāmanā ((meritorious) dedication, transference)); 9. rejoicing (anumodanā (rejoicing (in others' merit))); 10. accomplishment (abhinirhāra); 11. utmost purity (atyanta-viśuddhi) — these eleven dharmas characterize the knowledge of the paths, as shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // The dimming [of the gods] and the rest; the paths of the disciples and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas]; the greatly beneficial path of seeing, with its qualities both for this world and the next; // the function and resolute faith; [the resolute one] praised, eulogized, and lauded; the two supreme mental engagements in dedication and rejoicing; // accomplishment, and utmost purity — this is the path of cultivation of the wise bodhisattvas, as taught [under the rubric of] the knowledge of the paths. //
**II.A.ii.1**
1. The dimming [of the gods] and the rest (dhyāmīkaraṇatā etc.). The whole definition and so forth of these limbs of the knowledge of the paths is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // The dimming [of the gods'] radiance with respect to their fitness [for the teaching]; the fixed object, the pervasion, the nature of it, and the function. // Definition: the qualities that complete the knowledge of the paths and form its constituent parts are the limbs of the knowledge of the paths — that is the definition. Or else: the qualities present in a being's continuum, explicitly indicated at this stage as completing the knowledge of the paths, are its limbs. Divisions: the five limbs of the knowledge of the paths, beginning with the dimming, are these: the basis — the absence of manifest egotism; the cooperating condition — the arising of bodhicitta; the pervasion together with its cause; the nature — not forsaking saṃsāra; and the taking-in of beings not previously taken in. Scope: in general its range extends from before entering the path up to the buddha-ground; from the standpoint of the explicitly indicated limbs, its range extends from the path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**II.A.ii.2**
2. The path of the śrāvakas (śrāvaka-mārga). The definition and so forth of the realisation of the śrāvaka path is well shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in the verse written below. Thus: // Through the non-apprehension of the aspects of the four noble truths — this is the path of the śrāvakas, to be known within the way of the knowledge of the paths. // Definition: in order to favour disciples of śrāvaka type, the noble Mahāyāna realisation of śrāvaka-realisation type — established by the view that directly realises some one of the sixteen aspects (impermanence and the rest), taking as object some one of the four noble truths (suffering and the rest) — is the knowledge of the śrāvaka path, [a form of] the knowledge of the paths. Divisions: by way of aspects it is sixteenfold; by way of path it is threefold, by the division into the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. Scope: its range extends from the path of seeing up to the buddha-ground. According to some, its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the buddha-ground.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.ii.3**
3. The path of the pratyekabuddhas (pratyekabuddha-mārga). The whole definition and so forth of pratyekabuddha-realisation is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // Because of [their] awakening on their own, the self-arisen [pratyekabuddhas] have no need of others' instruction; and the profundity of the rhinoceros-like ones' knowledge is proclaimed. // For whomever there is a wish to hear, for whatever purpose, wherever, and in whatever manner — that very purpose becomes manifest, even without words, there and thus, accordingly. // Through abandoning the conceptualization of the apprehended object, but without abandoning the apprehender, and from [their] basis — the summary of the rhinoceros-path is to be understood. // Definition: in order to favour disciples of pratyekabuddha lineage, the noble Mahāyāna realisation of pratyekabuddha-realisation type — established by the view of the knowledge that directly realises the emptiness of the external apprehended object, taking the twelve sense-bases as object — is the knowledge of the pratyekabuddha path, [a form of] the knowledge of the paths. Divisions: it has three — the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha-ground.
**II.A.ii.4**
4. The Mahāyāna path of seeing (mahāyāna-darśana-mārga). Three things are to be known about the greatly beneficial path of seeing, set forth here in brief: its definition, divisions, and scope. Its nature is shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in five verses. Definition: the realisation of the truths, marked by the cessation of the two extremes of existence and quiescence, is the Mahāyāna path of seeing — that is its definition. Divisions: it has two — the knowledge [in meditative] equipoise and the subsequently-attained knowledge. From the standpoint of knowledge, the path of seeing is three knowledges: first, that which knows the śrāvaka path qua path of seeing; second, that which knows the pratyekabuddha path; third, that which knows the Mahāyāna path — these are the three divisions. From the standpoint of object and of differentiation, eight forbearances and eight knowledges — these sixteen divisions are to be understood. Scope: its pervasion occurs only on the first bodhisattva ground.
**II.A.ii.5**
5. The function of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-kāritra). The definition and so forth of the functions of the path of cultivation is clearly shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // The subduing in every way, named [thus]; the conquest of the afflictions in every way; invincibility to assault; awakening; and being worthy of worship as a basis. // Definition: the benefit attained by the power of cultivating reality [once] seen is the definition of the function of the path of cultivation. Divisions: it has six, namely: the function of subduing, by rejecting self-exaltation; the function of being beloved by all people; the function of overcoming the afflictions, attachment and the rest; the function of invincibility to assault, [withstanding] the impact of others' enmity and opposition; the function of progress toward perfect awakening; and the function of being worthy of worship as the locus and object of the Perfection of Wisdom. Scope: its range extends from the first ground up to the tenth ground. [On the path of cultivation in general:] Definition: the Mahāyāna subsequent realisation is the Mahāyāna path of cultivation — that is the definition. 'Subsequent realisation' and 'path of cultivation' are synonyms. Divisions: it has two — the contaminated path of cultivation and the uncontaminated path of cultivation. The contaminated is the conceptual path of cultivation; the uncontaminated is the non-conceptual. The contaminated is threefold, marked by the mental engagements of resolute faith, dedication, and rejoicing; the uncontaminated is twofold, having the nature of accomplishment and of utmost purity.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.ii.6**
6. Resolute faith of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-adhimukti). The whole definition and so forth of the path of cultivation that is resolute faith is clearly shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // Resolute faith is to be known as threefold: for one's own sake, for one's own and others' sake, and for others' sake alone; and each of these is held to be threefold. // [Each is] weak, middling, and strong; and by the further division into weak-weak and so on, each of these again is threefold — so it is held to be twenty-sevenfold. // Definition: the conceptual Mahāyāna subsequent realisation, established by the force of firm confidence in the Mother of the Conquerors, which is the source of one's own benefit, of one's own and others' benefit, and of others' benefit — the path of cultivation called resolute faith — that is the definition. Divisions: resolute faith is threefold by its root division — for one's own sake, for one's own and others' sake, and for others' sake. Though threefold, by the division into weak, middling, and strong it becomes ninefold (three threes). And this ninefold resolute faith, each [type] further divided by weak-weak and so forth, becomes twenty-sevenfold (nine times three), namely: weak-weak, weak-middling, weak-strong; middling-weak, middling-middling, middling-strong; strong-weak, strong-middling, strong-strong — these are the nine types of resolute faith for one's own sake; likewise are to be understood [the nine each] for one's own-and-others' sake and for others' sake. Scope: its range extends from the first ground up to the tenth ground. Some say from the second ground up to the tenth ground.
**II.A.ii.7**
7. The praise, eulogy, and laudation of one with resolute faith on the path of cultivation (stuti, stobha, praśaṃsā). The definition and so forth of the praise and the rest [bestowed on] the bodhisattva with resolute faith on the path of cultivation is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // Praise, eulogy, and laudation toward the Perfection of Wisdom are held [to be given] by three sets of nine, for [each of] the degrees of resolute faith. // Definition: the praise and the rest performed in regard to the resolute faith of the bodhisattva who cultivates it and is engaged in the aforesaid threefold resolute faith toward the Perfection of Wisdom — done in order to increase his enthusiasm — are marked by the realisation of the real meaning, not of the nature of mere eulogistic flattery; that is the definition. Divisions: as before, just twenty-seven sub-types. Scope: as for the path of cultivation that is resolute faith.
**II.A.ii.8**
8. Dedication on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-pariṇāmanā). The whole nature of this dedication — definition, divisions, and so forth — is clearly shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // Dedication is the special [mental engagement]; its function is supreme; it has the form of non-apprehension, and is marked by being free of error; // it is isolated [from signs], its scope being mindfulness whose nature is the flood of the buddhas' merit; it possesses means, it is signless, and it is approved by the buddhas; // not falling into the three realms; and another threefold dedication — weak, middling, and strong — whose nature is the rising of great merit. // Definition: the conceptual Mahāyāna subsequent realisation which dedicates the meritorious actions, one's own and others' wholesome [deeds], toward unsurpassed perfect awakening — that Mahāyāna path of cultivation called dedication is the definition. Divisions: this path of cultivation is twelvefold, namely the mental engagements of: special dedication, dedication with the form of non-apprehension, dedication marked by freedom from error, isolated dedication, dedication that is mindful recollection of [merit] whose nature is the flood of the buddhas' merit, dedication that is skill in means, signless dedication, dedication approved (rejoiced in) by the buddhas, dedication not contained in the three realms, and the weak, middling, and strong dedications whose nature is the rising of great merit — these are the twelve divisions. Scope: the range of this mental engagement of dedication extends from the first ground (the Joyous) up to the tenth ground.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.ii.9**
9. Rejoicing on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārgīya-anumodanā). The definition, divisions, and so forth of the mental engagement of rejoicing is described in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in just one verse. Thus: // By way of means and non-apprehension, the rejoicing in [others'] roots of virtue — the cultivation of the mental engagement of rejoicing is here prescribed. // Definition: the conceptual Mahāyāna subsequent realisation which rejoices in the meritorious actions, one's own and others' wholesome [deeds] — that Mahāyāna path of cultivation called rejoicing is the definition. Divisions: the mental engagement of rejoicing has two — rejoicing in one's own meritorious actions, and rejoicing in others' meritorious actions. Or else: the mental engagement of rejoicing that has the conventional as its object, and that which has the ultimate as its object. Scope: the ground-range of the three mental engagements — resolute faith, dedication, and rejoicing — is the same.
**II.A.ii.10**
10. Accomplishment (abhinirhāra). The definition and so forth of the uncontaminated path of cultivation that is accomplishment is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // Its nature, its supremacy, its non-fabrication of all [things], its consigning [of dharmas] by non-apprehension of dharmas, and its great purposefulness. // Definition: the uncontaminated Mahāyāna subsequent realisation which establishes the task of attaining the ultimate — that Mahāyāna path of cultivation called accomplishment is the definition. Divisions: it has five, namely: the unerring vision of all dharmas (form and the rest) is its nature; the supremacy of the path of cultivation, [in that] buddhahood is not attained otherwise; the non-fabrication that is the application to attainment, by not producing any distinctions among dharmas; the consigning [of dharmas] through the ultimate non-apprehension of all dharmas; and great purposefulness, from accomplishing the great purpose of buddhahood. Scope: the range of this accomplishment extends from the first ground up to the tenth ground.
**II.A.ii.11**
11. Utmost purity (atyanta-viśuddhi). The whole definition and so forth of the uncontaminated path of cultivation called utmost purity is very clearly set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // The purity of the fruit and the purity of form and the rest — because these two are undivided and uncut, [their] purity is proclaimed. // Through the abandoning of the threefold [obscuration] — afflictive, cognitive, and path — by the disciples, the rhinoceros-like ones, and the sons of the Conqueror, [there is purity]; but the purity of a Buddha is utmost, at all times. // The weak-weak and so forth path is the purity on the nine grounds, by way of being the antidote to the strong-strong and so forth defilement. // Definition: the uncontaminated Mahāyāna subsequent realisation which establishes the task of the final abandoning — that Mahāyāna path of cultivation called utmost purity is the definition. Divisions: the nine paths of cultivation, weak-weak and the rest, which are the antidotes to the nine antitheses to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, are the divisions of this path of cultivation that is utmost purity. Scope: the range of this path of cultivation extends from the first ground up to the tenth ground. // Thus the eleven dharmas characterizing the knowledge of the paths. //
**II.A.iii.intro**
(i) The nine dharmas characterizing the knowledge of the bases. They are: 1. by wisdom, no abiding in [cyclic] existence; 2. by compassion, no abiding in quiescence; 3. through lack of means, distance from the Mother of the Conquerors; 4. through means, nearness [to her]; 5. the antithesis (vipakṣa); 6. the antidote (pratipakṣa); 7. application (prayoga); 8. sameness (samatā); 9. the path of seeing — these nine dharmas characterize the knowledge of the bases, well stated in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // By wisdom, no abiding in existence; by compassion, no remaining in quiescence; through lack of means, distance; through means, nearness; // and the antithesis and antidote, application, and its sameness; the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and the rest — so the knowledge of the bases is presented. //

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.iii.1-2**
1. By wisdom, no abiding in existence. 2. By compassion, no abiding in quiescence. The definition and so forth of both is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // Abiding neither on the near shore nor on the far shore nor in between the two, by the knowledge of the sameness of the [three] times, the Perfection of Wisdom is held [to be]. // [By wisdom, no abiding in existence:] Definition: the wisdom present in a noble Mahāyāna practitioner's continuum, of hīnayāna type, having great compassion as its core, directly realising the sixteen aspects (impermanence and the rest), is the definition of this [aspect of the] knowledge of bases. And this Perfection of Wisdom of the bodhisattvas, because by wisdom it sees the faults of saṃsāra, does not abide in the existence-extreme of saṃsāra. Divisions: it has three — the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. [By compassion, no abiding in quiescence:] Definition: the Mahāyāna realisation which, by great compassion, turns back from the quiescence-extreme that disregards the conventional, is the definition of this [aspect of the] knowledge of bases. And this Perfection of Wisdom, because by compassion it acts for the welfare of beings, does not abide in the quiescence-extreme of nirvāṇa. Divisions: the three great compassions of the Mahāyāna noble one — that which has beings as object, that which has dharmas as object, and that which has no object — and the [other] divisions beginning with the arising of bodhicitta. [Of both:] because of realising the equality, in the mode of non-arising, of the dharmas of the three times, the bodhisattvas' Perfection of Wisdom, remote [from others] in that it is beyond the range of śrāvakas and the rest, abides neither on the near shore (saṃsāra) nor on the far shore (nirvāṇa); nor does it abide in between, since apart from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa there is no [third] entity — because, through the correct penetration of wisdom and compassion, it is free of apprehending either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Scope: the range of both extends from the first ground (the Joyous) up to the buddha-ground.
**II.A.iii.3**
3. Distance through lack of means (anupāyena dūratvam). Its whole definition and so forth is clearly set down in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in half a verse. Thus: // Through lack of means, it [the knowledge of bases of the śrāvakas] is distant, because of apprehension with signs. // Definition: the knowledge of the śrāvakas and the rest, which directly realises the aspects (impermanence and the rest) but, lacking the knowledge of the sameness of the [three] times, operates through apprehension with signs, and so, deficient in compassion and wisdom, has become distant from the Mother of the Conquerors — that is the definition. Divisions: two — the knowledge of the aspects (impermanence and the rest) present in the śrāvaka's continuum, and that present in the pratyekabuddha's continuum. Scope: its range extends from the path of seeing up to the stage of arhatship.
**II.A.iii.4**
4. Nearness through means (upāyena avidūratā). The setting-forth of its definition and so forth is well done in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in half a verse. Thus: // Through skill in means, its proper nearness to her [the Mother] is taught. // Definition: the knowledge of the aspects (impermanence and the rest), of hīnayāna type, of the noble Mahāyāna practitioners, taken up by great compassion and by the wisdom directly realising emptiness, is its definition. "For the bodhisattvas and the rest, who have discarded the signs of the deluded clinging to the reality [of things], the very full understanding of all dharmas (form and the rest) is the full understanding of their sameness; hence there is proper nearness to the Mother, it should be understood." Divisions: it has three — the Mahāyāna paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha-ground.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.iii.5**
5. The antithesis (vipakṣa). Its definition and so forth is very clearly set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in one verse. Thus: // The notion of [substantial] practice — regarding the emptiness of the form-aggregate and the rest, regarding dharmas of the three times, regarding giving and the rest, regarding the limbs of awakening — is the antithetical [knowledge]. // Definition: the hīnayāna knowledge of bases, divorced from great compassion and from the wisdom of emptiness, having the nature of apprehending [things as substantially] existent — that is the definition. "All [things] — form and the rest, and the dharmas of the three times, whether placed among the contaminated or uncontaminated, whose very nature is non-apprehension — are seen [by such knowledge] everywhere through the apprehension of [substantial] existence, as empty of the self and the rest imputed by others. But their notion of [substantial] practice, although it is an antidote [to other faults], being engaged through error and therefore to be abandoned, becomes the antithesis." Divisions and scope: both its divisions and scope are to be understood just as shown in the section on 'distance through lack of means.'
**II.A.iii.6**
6. The antidote (pratipakṣa). Its whole definition, divisions, and so forth is shown at length in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in three verses. Thus: // The absence of egotism in giving and the rest; the setting of others in that [practice]; the prohibition of the extreme of attachment — yet there is a subtle attachment with respect to the Conquerors and the rest; // its profundity, by reason of the natural isolation of the course of dharmas; the knowledge that dharmas are of a single nature; the avoidance of attachment; // through the prohibition of [the views] 'seen' and the rest, its hard-to-fathom character is taught; because [the Mother] is not cognized by form and the rest, its inconceivability is asserted. // Definition: the knowledge of bases present in a noble Mahāyāna practitioner's continuum, taken up by great compassion as means and by the wisdom directly realising emptiness, has the nature of the antidote — that is its definition. Divisions and scope: both are to be understood just as described earlier in the context of 'nearness through means.' [Special note:] there are two divisions of the knowledge of bases (sarvajñatā), [namely] distance and nearness to the Mother of the Conquerors. 'Nearness to the Mother,' 'nearness through skill in means,' 'antidote,' and 'Mahāyāna knowledge of bases' — these four are synonyms. 'Distance from the resultant Mother of the Conquerors,' 'distance through lack of means,' 'being bound by the grasping that apprehends signs,' 'antithesis,' and 'hīnayāna knowledge of bases' — these are synonyms. This division of antithesis and antidote for the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the rest is to be understood just as indicated. As it is said: // Having done thus, [these] as stated are to be known within the way of the knowledge of bases; this is the complete division of antithesis and antidote. // Moreover: "Thus, for the śrāvakas and the rest, their practice, through being distant from the Mother, although it is an antidote, being engaged in the error of apprehending [substantial] things, is for the bodhisattvas to be discarded, and hence an antithesis."
**II.A.iii.7**
7. Application (prayoga). Its whole definition, divisions, and so forth is set forth at length in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in a verse-passage of two and a half [verses]. Thus: // The application of practice — with respect to form and the rest, with respect to their impermanence and the rest, with respect to their non-filling and filling, and with respect to their non-attachment — by way of prohibition; // [the application of] non-alteration and of non-agency; the threefold difficult application; [the application] that is non-futile in attaining the fruit according to capacity, and [the application] that is desired; // and that which is independent of other conditions, the sevenfold knower of manifestation. // Definition: the yoga of a being, of hīnayāna type, which is the antidote to the clinging-apprehension engaged in error with respect to the conventional nature of things and their distinctions, is the application — that is its definition. Divisions: application is tenfold, namely: the prohibition of clinging to form and the rest as [truly] real; the prohibition of clinging to their distinctions (impermanence and the rest) as [truly] real; the non-filling with respect to imagined forms; the filling with respect to the forms of true nature; the ultimate non-decline and non-increase (non-alteration) with respect to the perfections; ultimate non-agency; the difficulty of the aim-application-function, respectively, of [the three] which have the three knowledges as their nature; the non-futility through attaining the fruit according to capacity; the independence from other conditions in the greatly beneficial awakening; and the sevenfold knowledge of manifestation beginning with dedication that is like a dream — these are the ten divisions. Scope: its range extends from the path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.A.iii.8**
8. Sameness (samatā). Its nature is shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in half a verse. Thus: // The fourfold non-imagining of that, with respect to form and the rest, is held to be sameness. // Definition: the non-imagining of the cognizer-and-cognized dharmas that are the aspects of the aforesaid tenfold application of the knowledge of bases is the definition of sameness. Divisions: in each of the aforesaid tenfold applications there are four non-imaginings; thus the sub-types of this sameness number forty. And it is said in the Ālokā commentary: "Thus, by the prohibition of [four kinds of] imagining — the imagining of the objects form and the rest; the imagining of the signs blue and the rest; the discursive imagining beginning with 'form is twofold, twentyfold'; and the imagining of attainments beginning with the roots conducive to penetration — the non-apprehension of the cognizer-and-cognized dharmas is taught as fourfold, it should be understood." Scope: the range of this sameness extends from the path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.
**II.A.iii.9**
9. The path of seeing (darśana-mārga). Its whole definition and so forth is set forth in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in five verses. Definition: the realisation of the truths that is empty of the thirty-two superimpositions is the path of seeing — that is its definition. Divisions: by the differentiation of the three paths of seeing of the three vehicles, its sixteen moments are its sixteen divisions. // Thus the nine dharmas characterizing the knowledge of the bases. //
**II.B.intro**
2. The thirty-six dharmas characterizing the four applications. Therein: eleven dharmas characterize the full realisation of all aspects, eight characterize the culminating realisation, thirteen characterize the serial realisation, and four characterize the realisation in a single instant — making thirty-six.
**II.B.i.intro**
(a) The eleven dharmas characterizing the full realisation of all aspects. They are: 1. the aspects (ākāra); 2. the applications (prayoga); 3. the qualities (guṇa); 4. the faults (doṣa); 5. the marks (lakṣaṇa); 6. the [roots] conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya); 7. the [roots] conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya); 8. the irreversible community (avaivartika gaṇa); 9. the sameness of existence and quiescence; 10. the unsurpassed purification of the [buddha-]field; 11. skill in means — these eleven dharmas characterize the full realisation of all aspects, as shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in two verses. Thus: // The aspects together with the applications, the qualities, the faults, together with the marks; the [roots] conducive to liberation and to penetration; the learner [community], the irreversible community; // and the sameness of existence and quiescence, the unsurpassed purity of the [buddha-]field — this full realisation of all aspects, together with skill in means. // Definition: the yoga of a being, established as taken up by the wisdom consisting of meditative cultivation, [directed at] the 173 aspects connected with the three knowledges, is the full realisation of all aspects — that is its definition. Synonyms: 'the bodhisattva path,' 'the path of the perfections,' 'the yoga of a being,' 'the application of the knowledge of aspects,' 'the application of the knowledge of the paths,' and 'the armour-practice' are synonyms. Divisions: from the standpoint of aspects, 173; from the standpoint of applications, twenty. Scope: its range extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the stage of the bodhisattva at the final moment.

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.B.i.1**
1. The aspects (ākāra). The whole definition and so forth of the aspects is well described at length in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in five verses. Definition: the distinction of cultivation-application, [directed] at the aspects of the three knowledges, by way of comprising the knowledge of all aspects, the path, and the bases, is the definition of the aspects. Divisions: the aspects have 173 divisions, namely: twenty-seven of the knowledge of bases, thirty-six of the knowledge of the paths, and 110 of the knowledge of all aspects — making 173. Of the four noble truths, four [aspects] for each of the first three truths makes twelve, and fifteen for the fourth, the truth of the path — so the knowledge of bases has twenty-seven aspects. As stated in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra: // Beginning with the aspect of non-existence up to the aspect of immovability — these are four per truth, and fifteen are reckoned for the path. // Eight for the truth of origin, seven for the truth of the path, five for the truth of suffering, and sixteen for the truth of cessation — so the knowledge of the paths has thirty-six aspects. As stated in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra: // For origin, path, suffering, and cessation respectively, they are proclaimed as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. // The thirty-seven limbs of awakening are the aspects of the knowledge of bases [shared] with the learner-śrāvakas; thirty-four are [the aspects] of the knowledge of the paths of the bodhisattvas; thirty-nine uncommon ones are [the aspects] of the buddhas' knowledge of all aspects — so the knowledge of all aspects has 110 aspects. As stated in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra: // Beginning with the applications of mindfulness and ending with the aspect of buddhahood, for the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the buddhas respectively, // they are held to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, thirty-nine, and nine, by the division of the three [kinds of] omniscience, in accordance with the truth of the path. // Since the object-aspects are to be understood before the knowledge-aspects, the 173 object-aspects are shown first.
**II.B.i.2**
2. The applications (prayoga). The definition and so forth of the applications is described at length and very clearly in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in four verses. Definition: the very knowledge — having the nature of the cultivation that is the union of calm-abiding and insight, [directed] at the cognizer and cognized and at the aspects of the bases and of the path, and having the character of essencelessness and freedom from elaboration — is here the definition of the explicitly indicated application. Or else: the yoga of a being, taken up by the wisdom consisting of the cultivation that is the union of calm-abiding and insight, [directed] at all the aspects of the three knowledges, is here the definition of the indicated application. Divisions: the applications have twenty divisions: by nature, five; from the standpoint of the supporting person, eight; from the standpoint of the means of perfecting the cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom, four; from the standpoint of the fruit of application, two; and from the standpoint of swift cultivation, one — making twenty. By nature, five: the application of non-abiding (in form and the rest, by essencelessness); the application of non-application (since application to them is no application at all); the profound application (in the section on the knowledge of bases, by reason of the non-apprehension of a foundation, owing to the profundity of the suchness of form and the rest); the hard-to-fathom application (in the section on the knowledge of the paths, by reason of the naturally undisturbed character, owing to the hard-to-fathom nature of form and the rest); and the immeasurable application (in the section on the knowledge of all aspects, by reason of the non-apprehension of any limit, owing to the immeasurability of form and the rest). From the standpoint of the supporting person, eight: the application of awakening with difficulty over a long time (of the beginner prone to fear in profound emptiness); the application of obtaining the prophecy (from the heat-realisation of the path of preparation onward, there is no terror at the profound true nature, nor estrangement from the practice of the six perfections even in dreams); the irreversible application (from the summit-realisation onward, by long habituation in realising the true nature); the issuing-forth application (from forbearance onward, by skill in means, through the firmness of realising the true nature, abandoning the dharmas that obstruct toward the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha [vehicles]); the uninterrupted application (from the supreme-dharma-realisation onward, by the power of uninterrupted application through continuous cultivation, there is the certainty of nearness to the direct vision of the dharmadhātu, like the nearness of the great ocean); the application of nearness to awakening (by the practice of being the support of the fresh uncontaminated dharmas that are the causes of omniscience); the application of swift awakening (by swiftly accomplishing the fruit, the Dharma-body); and the application for others' welfare (turning the wheel of Dharma and the rest). From the standpoint of means, four: the application of non-increase-and-non-decline (since, ultimately, no increase or decline of qualities and faults is seen, one is sanctioned in coursing in the Perfection of Wisdom); the application of the non-apprehension of dharma, non-dharma, and the rest (by the practice of, ultimately, not apprehending dharma, non-dharma, and the rest); the inconceivable application (form and the rest being inconceivable, since they have the nature of the dharmadhātu); and the non-conceptual application (since, form and the rest having the nature of the dharmadhātu, there is no conceptualization of form, its sign, its nature, and so forth). From the standpoint of fruit, two: the application of bestowing the jewel of the fruit (since it bestows the jewel of the fruit, [the stages] from stream-entry up to unsurpassed perfect awakening); and the application of purification (since it is the cause of abandoning the afflictive and cognitive obscurations). From the standpoint of swift cultivation, one: the application of the [time-]limit (since it is the nature of things that great jewels have many obstacles, the writing-down of the Mother — whose nature is the supreme jewel — though it has many obstacles over a year, is yet swift).

title: Abhisamayālaṅkāravivaraṇa
text:
**II.B.i.3**
3. The qualities (guṇa). The whole definition and so forth of the qualities is shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in half a verse. Thus: // The destruction of the power of the Māras and the rest is the fourteenfold quality. // Definition: the excellence attained by the power of cultivating the applications is the definition of the qualities. Divisions: the qualities have fourteen divisions, namely: the quality of destroying the power of the Māras (when the perfection is being taken up, the obstacles made by the Māras are warded off by the power of the Tathāgatas); the quality of being known to the buddhas' attention (since, in the preparatory, main, and concluding stages of application, one gains the attention of the Tathāgatas); the quality of being made manifest to the buddhas (since one gains the buddhas' knowledge-vision); the quality of nearness to perfect awakening (by gaining the proximity of the Tathāgatas); the quality of great purposefulness and the rest (by gaining great benefit); the quality of determining the [right] place (by gaining the quality of determining the place [for teaching], doing the Tathāgatas' work); the quality of fulfilling all uncontaminated dharmas (by gaining the fulfilment of the antidote-dharmas); the quality of being a person of [authoritative] speech (by gaining the ability to speak the discourse of the knowledge of all aspects); the quality of indivisibility (by gaining the protection of the Tathāgatas); the quality of producing uncommon roots of virtue (by accomplishing vast joy); the quality of accomplishing the truthfulness of one's vow (when, in the rejoicing-in-vows, one gradually accomplishes the conformity of the vow to reality through the practice of application); the quality of taking hold of the lofty fruit (by resolute faith in the profound and lofty meaning); the quality of accomplishing the welfare of beings (by gaining the capacity to act for beings' welfare); and the quality of attaining certainty (by the practice of application when endowed with the roots of virtue that bring about the unimpaired Perfection of Wisdom) — these are the fourteen qualities.
**II.B.i.4**
4. The faults (doṣa). The faults of the applications are shown in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra in half a verse. Thus: // And six faults are to be recognized, together with four sets of ten. // Definition: the obstructions that hinder the arising, persistence, intensification, and progress of the applications are the faults — that is the definition. Divisions: the faults have forty-six divisions. The first set of ten: attaining [the perfection] with difficulty (slow inspiration in the Mother); too-swift inspiration; bodily badness; mental badness; reciting and the like done improperly; grasping the signs of aversion; loss of the cause; loss of the relish of the sublime; loss of the supreme vehicle; and loss of the aim — these ten. The second set of ten: loss of the connection of cause and fruit; loss of the unsurpassed station; the arising of inspiration that conceptualizes manifold objects; clinging to the writing of syllables; clinging to non-existence; clinging to syllables; clinging to non-syllables; attending to one's homeland and the like; relishing gain, honour, and fame; and seeking skill-in-means on the wrong path — these ten. These twenty faults are set forth as obstacles to the practitioner engaged in the perfection. Now, in turn, the incompatibility that arises in [teacher-student] engagement is explained. The third set of ten: discordance of zeal and indolence [between hearer and speaker — this is a fault of both]; discordance in the object of zeal [likewise of both]; discordance of having few wants and many wants; the [mis]match of practising and not practising the ascetic virtues; being of good or bad character; generosity and stinginess; accepting or not accepting a gift; being a quick-witted or a needs-elaboration learner; being expert or not expert in the dharma of the sūtras and the rest; and being endowed or not endowed with the six perfections — these ten. The fourth set of ten: skill or lack of skill in means; obtaining or not obtaining the retention-formulae; wishing or not wishing to write [it] down; being free or not free from desire and the like — these four; aversion to the way of [skilful] means; and gladness at going to a happy destiny — these two; one or other of the hearer and speaker delighting in solitary assembly; not giving an opportunity to one who wishes to follow; longing for some material trifle and [un]willingness to give it; and going in a direction that is or is not an obstacle to life — these four; making ten. The remaining set of six faults: going to or coming from a famine-stricken region; going to or coming from a region troubled by bandits and the like; the despondency of [excessive] attention to families — these three; the application that creates Māra-induced division; the introduction of a counterfeit [teaching] (presenting something fabricated); and the arousing of longing for an unsuitable object — these other three; making six. Thus there are forty-six faults in all.
